title: The trusted operating layer behind every Aloha AI system
summary: A governed platform for organizations, projects, evidence, guardrails, approvals, integrations, and append-only audit events.
audience: Organizations operating evidence-sensitive or regulated AI workflows.
implementationStatus: Core workflow, adapter, gateway, and twin SDK foundations are implemented; production integrations remain engagement-specific.
licensing: Available through scoped implementations, pilots, and licensed platform engagements.
methodology: Bind work to an organization and project
assumptions: Organizations configure appropriate access, evidence, and review authority
limitations: Public pages demonstrate architecture and do not expose authenticated client data
Production behavior depends on configured integrations

title: AI adoption, content systems, regulatory intelligence, and legal AI workflow
summary: The integrated Aloha AI practice for building evidence-grounded systems around how people actually trust, review, and use AI.
audience: Organizations in regulated innovation sectors that need credible AI implementation and public-facing intelligence.
implementationStatus: Active consulting and product practice supported by published methods, live builds, and canonical resources.
changelog: 2026-07: practice consolidated into the canonical resource graph
licensing: Engagement and product terms are defined in individual scopes and agreements.
methodology: Locate the decision or workflow bottleneck
Ground the work in primary evidence
assumptions: The organization can identify a real decision, workflow, or evidence problem
limitations: The practice is not a substitute for licensed advice outside an agreed scope

title: What a real AI stack looks like for your work
summary: Role-specific blueprints that map monitoring, evidence, knowledge, generation, review, and operations into one defensible system.
audience: Teams choosing the AI layers that fit their work rather than buying disconnected tools.

collection.heading: Choose the stack that matches your work

evidence: Canonical services, tools, monitors, and methods
methodology: Separate the work into functional layers
Map each layer to a bounded resource
Name failure modes and human gates
assumptions: Teams want a system blueprint rather than a single model recommendation
limitations: Each stack requires adaptation to actual authority, data, budget, and risk

title: Founder / Startup AI Stack
summary: A five-layer system for policy monitoring, product-claim review, internal knowledge, customer education, and diligence preparation.
audience: Founders and small startup teams working without large compliance or operations departments.
assumptions: A small team needs leverage without pretending risk disappears
limitations: The blueprint must be adapted to sector and financing stage

title: Law Firm AI Stack
summary: Six connected layers for legal research, internal knowledge, client alerts, drafting support, citation verification, intake, and operations.
audience: Law firms and legal teams building reviewable AI workflows.
assumptions: Licensed professionals retain responsibility for legal work
limitations: The stack does not practice law or replace attorney judgment

title: Policy & Advocacy AI Stack
summary: A primary-source stack for legislative monitoring, testimony and briefing support, coalition research, and public education.
audience: Policy, advocacy, coalition, and public-interest teams.
assumptions: The team can define its jurisdiction and policy objective
limitations: Monitoring coverage and legal interpretation require jurisdiction-specific review

title: Psychedelic / Cannabis Intelligence AI Stack
summary: A four-layer stack for scheduling, state status, claim substantiation, and platform-suppression intelligence in fast-moving psychoactive-plant markets.
audience: Cannabis, psychedelics, and psychoactive-plant operators and researchers.
assumptions: The market and jurisdictions are explicitly scoped
limitations: Regulatory status can change rapidly and requires current verification

title: Research Lab / Academic AI Stack
summary: A five-layer evidence system for literature review, evidence matrices, notes, publication support, and policy translation.
audience: Research labs, academic teams, and evidence-intensive scholars.
assumptions: The lab defines inclusion, exclusion, and review criteria
limitations: AI-assisted synthesis cannot substitute for methodological judgment

title: Your expertise, turned into a system that never starts from a blank page
summary: A research-to-publication system for authors, researchers, newsletter writers, and expert firms whose reputation depends on grounded, voice-true work.
audience: Content-heavy experts and boutique firms whose expertise is the product.
implementationStatus: Available as a scoped discovery, build, handoff, and keep-current engagement.
roadmap: Add reusable evidence and voice evaluations
licensing: Built and licensed through a defined client scope.
assumptions: The expert can provide an authoritative source record and representative writing
limitations: No system can infer an authentic voice from insufficient source material

title: AI Content System for Regulated Organizations
summary: A production framework that keeps AI-assisted content grounded, on-voice, reviewable, and auditable at scale.
audience: Regulated and reputation-sensitive organizations producing AI-assisted content.
implementationStatus: Published implementation framework within the Regulated Trust Stack.
assumptions: The organization maintains approved source material
limitations: The framework requires accountable reviewers and current source governance

title: EDSA — The Neuroscience-of-Trust Content Architecture
summary: A framework for designing regulated content that serves human comprehension and platform classification without sacrificing evidence.
audience: Regulated creators, educators, and communications teams.
implementationStatus: Published analytical framework with ongoing application testing.
assumptions: Content must be understandable without becoming misleading
limitations: Platform behavior is not fully observable and neuroscience does not predict individual response

title: Oregon SB 303 Psilocybin Compliance Kit

audience: Oregon psilocybin operators and compliance teams.
implementationStatus: Published compliance-intelligence framework; operational configuration requires current authority and counsel review.

title: Platform Suppression Monitoring Playbook
summary: A disciplined monitoring framework for detecting, documenting, and responding to quiet distribution and reach suppression.
audience: Regulated creators, brands, and advocacy organizations exposed to platform-risk.
implementationStatus: Published monitoring method with engagement-specific instrumentation available.

title: Is Your AI Twin Legally Exposed?
summary: A twenty-question directional self-screen across consent, disclosure, provenance, substantiation, platform conduct, and regulated-sector boundaries.
audience: Operators using AI twins, avatars, cloned voices, or synthetic-media agents.
implementationStatus: Public browser-local educational self-screen; answers are not transmitted.
evidence: Published consent, disclosure, provenance, advertising, platform, and professional-boundary rules
methodology: Route to governed resources and human review
assumptions: Responses accurately describe the deployed or planned twin
limitations: Not legal advice, not a compliance certification, and not a validated psychometric instrument
Current law and platform rules require independent verification

questions.prompt: Is every cloned voice or likeness backed by written, use-scoped consent?
Does the twin use a third party’s likeness or voice?
Does it replicate a deceased person’s likeness or voice?
Does consent define permitted uses and an expiry?
Does the twin disclose that it is AI at first contact?
Is a realistic replica disclosed as synthetic?
Is disclosure enforced by the system?
Do synthetic outputs carry machine-readable provenance?
Are platform AI-content labels applied?
Has provenance been verified after export and upload?
Are health, efficacy, or outcome claims substantiated before use?
Are claims about the AI system itself accurate and substantiated?
Are reviews and endorsements genuine and properly disclosed?
Is claim evidence gathered before a claim ships?
Does the twin scrape or automate messaging on LinkedIn?
Do marketing emails have a working opt-out that is honored?
Do emails use honest headers and a valid mailing address?
Does the twin operate in a licensed field?
Could it give legal or medical advice it is not licensed to give?
Do communications state boundaries and name the responsible licensed professional?
